entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giovanni Battista Ramusio (1485–1557) was a Venetian diplomat, geographer, and editor whose monumental three-volume work, *Navigationi et Viaggi* (Navigations and Travels), published between 1550 and 1559, became the foundational collection of European travel literature from the Age of Exploration. Serving the Republic of Venice as secretary to the Council of Ten and ambassador to France and other courts, Ramusio leveraged his extensive network and access to official documents to compile firsthand accounts of voyages that fundamentally reshaped Europe's understanding of the world, from the Americas to Asia. His meticulous editorial work and discerning selection of narratives made him a pivotal figure in the intellectual currents that defined the early modern period's global consciousness.

Ramusio's *Navigationi et Viaggi* systematically gathered and translated into Italian the most significant travelogues of his era and earlier periods. Volume I (1550) focused on Africa and the Indian Ocean, including accounts by Leo Africanus and Vasco da Gama. Volume II (1559, posthumous) was dedicated entirely to Marco Polo, providing one of the most comprehensive editions of his *Description of the World*. Volume III (1556) chronicled explorations of the Americas, featuring narratives by Christopher Columbus, Hernán Cortés, Giovanni da Verrazzano, and Jacques Cartier, among others. He often included maps and woodcut illustrations, enhancing the geographical and ethnographic detail for his readers.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Giovanni Battista Ramusio's *Navigationi et Viaggi* critically shaped European geographical understanding by compiling and disseminating primary accounts of global exploration, influencing subsequent cartography, trade, and colonial ventures. His work preserved invaluable historical documents and fueled the intellectual curiosity of the early modern period.
